sections.h2: What does a Woodbridge seller need to clear before closing?
sections.html:
Woodbridge Township skips the certificate of continued occupancy, yet a house still needs an alarm certificate and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection to close. The sewer check is where sellers stumble, because floor drains, sump pumps and downspouts tied into the sewer must be fixed first.

Woodbridge is also large and varied. Roughly 105,000 residents live across ten communities, from waterfront flood zones to older streets in the Rahway Valley and neighborhoods beside the highways, so one inspection list lands very differently from section to section.

sections.h2: What do the Woodbridge figures show about homes and renters?
sections.html:
The 2020 census recorded 103,639 residents, and the mid-2025 estimate is 104,802. On 23.26 square miles of land, owners occupy about 66 percent of homes, which leaves roughly a third of households renting.

sections.h2: Which of the ten Woodbridge communities is my house in?
sections.html:
Woodbridge Township is an umbrella over ten unincorporated communities. The Census Bureau tracks them as separate places, and their 2020 populations show the scale:

  • Iselin, 20,088 residents;
  • Woodbridge Proper, 19,839;
  • Colonia, 18,609;
  • Avenel, 16,290;
  • Fords, 12,941;
  • Port Reading, 3,921, with Keasbey, Sewaren, Hopelawn and Menlo Park Terrace making up the rest.

A mailing address may say Iselin or Colonia, but the municipality that bills the tax and requires the inspections is Woodbridge Township in every case. Woodbridge itself is the oldest original township in the state, granted a royal charter on June 1, 1669.

sections.h2: How do the Turnpike, the Parkway and the rail stations affect value here?
sections.html:
The New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway meet here, and the township houses the headquarters of the authority that operates both. The Parkway covers 7.5 miles of town between Exits 127 and 132, while the Turnpike crosses for about 5.25 miles and has Exit 11. With U.S. 1 and 9 and several state routes, the road network totals 303.32 miles, 244.16 of them municipal.

Three train stations serve the township. Metropark, on the Northeast Corridor, recorded 3,702 average weekday boardings in 2025, seventh highest on NJ Transit, with Amtrak service as well. Avenel and Woodbridge stations sit on the North Jersey Coast Line, and buses 115 and 116 head to Port Authority.

Houses near Metropark or a Parkway ramp suit commuters, while houses beside the highways face road noise, so describe both plainly in a listing.

The school district ran 25 schools for 13,836 students in 2022-23, including Colonia, John F. Kennedy Memorial and Woodbridge high schools and the RISE program.

sections.h2: How much does flood risk matter to a Woodbridge sale?
sections.html:
Per Wikipedia's summary of floodplain studies, about 19 percent of the township sits inside FEMA flood hazard areas. Water wraps three sides: the Arthur Kill to the east, the Raritan River to the south and the Rahway River to the north, and some built-up land lies only five feet above sea level.

Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 struck the Watson-Crampton area beside the Woodbridge River hard, and the township afterward used the state's buyout program to purchase and remove many homes in flood hazard areas. For a house near the Woodbridge River, Heards Brook, the Raritan in Keasbey, or the Arthur Kill in Sewaren and Port Reading, expect questions about flood zone status and insurance history.

Pull together your flood insurance policy, any elevation certificate and past claim records before listing. A cash buyer cares about the same facts but can price the risk straight into an offer.

sections.h2: Which inspections does Woodbridge require for a resale?
sections.html:
The township's certificate of compliance sheet says no Certificate of Continued Occupancy is required, but a smoke detector inspection applies under an ordinance from April 15, 1980, and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection under one from March 3, 1998. There is no online form, so you book by phone and need the buyer's name, address, email and phone number plus a closing date.

  • Smoke detectors must be on every level, mounted with screws, and battery models must be the ten-year sealed type since January 1, 2019.
  • Carbon monoxide detectors go within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • Open permits and violations must be closed before the inspector releases the certificate.
  • The owner or a representative has to be at the house for the visit.
  • The finished certificate stays valid for 60 days.

The sewer rules are where houses fail. The township's sanitary sewer page names the banned connections: roof drains and downspouts, basement floor drains, sump pumps, yard and driveway drains, and missing or cracked trap caps. Floor drains get plugged and covered with concrete, and sump pumps and downspouts must send water to the street rather than the sewer. Fix these before you request the inspection.

sections.h2: Where is a Woodbridge deed recorded, and when are taxes due?
sections.html:
Middlesex County records the deed at the County Clerk's Registry, 4th Floor of the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office stays open until 4:10 p.m. on weekdays, but you must be in line by 4. Appointments are optional, though booked customers go first. A deed must include the words "Prepared by," the tax block and lot and the consideration, and a paper filing with no cover sheet draws a $20 indexing charge.

Bills are mailed every January and July, with payment dates on the first day of every February, May, August and November. The Tax Collection Office, on the first floor of Town Hall at 1 Main Street, opens at 8:30 in the morning and closes at 4:30 on weekdays, staying open until 6:30 on Tuesdays. A drop box stands in front of Town Hall. Sewer has its own bill, with the second half due October 1, and the township counts the date it receives the money, not the postmark.

sections.h2: How should a Woodbridge owner choose between an agent, a solo sale and a cash buyer?
sections.html:
An agent listing suits a well-kept house in a strong section, a cash buyer suits one with flood, sewer or repair problems, and a solo sale fits an owner who can run showings and the contract. Sewer and flood questions often tip the balance here.

  • Use an agent if your sewer connections are clean and the house shows well.
  • Go solo if you will handle the inspections and the Middlesex County recording yourself or through an attorney.
  • Pick an as-is cash buyer if the house has an illegal sewer connection, flood damage in its past, open permits or tenants, since that buyer can absorb the cost.

Whatever you choose, book the township inspection once a closing date is set, and judge written offers by the amount you keep after the transfer fee, taxes and payoff.

faqs.q: Must a Woodbridge house have a certificate of occupancy to sell?
faqs.a: No. The township says a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required. A smoke and carbon monoxide inspection and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection are.

faqs.q: What does the sewer discharge inspection look for?
faqs.a: It checks that no roof drains, floor drains, sump pumps or yard drains feed the sanitary sewer and that trap caps are intact. An ordinance adopted March 3, 1998 requires it before a resale.

faqs.q: How long does a Woodbridge compliance certificate last?
faqs.a: Sixty days from the inspection. Time the visit so the certificate has not lapsed by closing.

faqs.q: When do Woodbridge tax installments fall due?
faqs.a: The first day of February, May, August and November. Bills are mailed in January and July, and payments are taken in Town Hall at 1 Main Street.

faqs.q: Which office records a Woodbridge deed?
faqs.a: The Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, on the fourth floor. Weekday service ends at 4:10 p.m., and you must arrive by 4.
